headline: The first surviving fiscal document is bilingual
evidence: PERF 558 records a tax down-payment in both Greek and Arabic on 25 April 643, showing a new ruling language beside an inherited documentary one.
limits: One receipt does not measure language prevalence or establish the first use of Arabic.

headline: Greek still carried provincial government
evidence: The archive of the local official Flavius Papas contains 107 texts; Foss reports that most are in Greek and many concern taxes and requisitions under Umayyad rule.
limits: The archive is one Upper Egyptian survival and is not a complete language census.

headline: Arabic entered an inherited fiscal office
evidence: Later narrative sources place al-Hajjaj's conversion of the Iraqi fiscal register from Persian to Arabic in 78 AH / 697 CE, using Persian-trained personnel; the underlying process was probably gradual.
limits: The narrative date is not a surviving register or proof of an instantaneous provincial switch.

headline: Arabic became the public language of imperial money
evidence: The reformed gold and silver coinage abandoned inherited figural types for epigraphic issues dominated by Arabic religious and mint inscriptions.
limits: Coin legends show public imperial language, not the working language of every office.

headline: Local government remained multilingual after reform
evidence: The Qurra ibn Sharik dossier includes official Greek, Arabic, and bilingual correspondence between Fustat and Aphrodito, alongside Coptic tax registers and security documents.
limits: A rich but local dossier does not establish language shares for Egypt or the wider caliphate.
